 As temperatures drop, many families across western Pennsylvania are facing a familiar winter dilemma: pay the heating bill or keep up with other expenses. State and local agencies say help is available through programs such as LIHEAP — the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program — but officials warn many eligible households still are not enrolled in assistance that could lower their costs or prevent a loss of heat.
 Local agencies say the need is already evident. LIHEAP can provide a one-time cash grant toward a household’s heating bill. A separate LIHEAP crisis grant can help when a heating system breaks down or when a family is at risk of losing heat.
 “We go to the house and do an assessment on it, get a contractor to come work on it. And then we would go back and do a safety test to make sure that unit is working correctly,” said Scott Zarefoss, Director of Weatherization at Tableland Services in Somerset County.
 He said the agency’s workload reflects ongoing demand. “On average over the last three years, we’ve done about 190 homes per year,” Zarefoss said.
 State data also shows the scale of need across the region. Last season, the 6 News 10 counties coverage area recorded more than 24,000 approved LIHEAP heating assistance applications and more than 18,000 approved crisis applications, according to the Department of Human Services. For the first two weeks of this season, DHS said it received more than 18,000 LIHEAP applications and approved more than 13,000.
 Zarefoss said unsafe heating practices can become a serious concern when families run out of options.
 “We go into homes that have people using their stoves or there are burners on their stove for heat. They’re using non-combustible kerosene heaters that produce toxic flames in the house,” he said. “So the health and safety is just as important as getting them heat in the house.”
 Additional help may be available through utility Customer Assistance Programs, known as CAP. Those programs can lower a customer’s monthly bill based on income and may put past-due balances on hold and forgive them over time.
 The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission says there is a “CAP gap” — people who qualify for these programs but are not enrolled. Officials say even people who are unsure whether they qualify should still reach out for help.
 Zarefoss encouraged residents to look beyond state programs as well.
 “There are a lot of local resources. There are some nonprofit agencies around, and there are several churches that have programs available that may be able to help people,” he said. “So I would just suggest call your community action agency and see if they have a list of those resources.”
 Residents can apply for LIHEAP online through DHS COMPASS or get a paper application from their county assistance office. The application also allows applicants to choose to share their information with their utility, which may help connect them with CAP and other programs.
